::: {.oneline}
A response function is the linear kernel connecting a weak external
perturbation to the change it produces in an observable — and its poles are the
excitations of the system.
:::

## Short answer

Switch on a weak perturbation $\hat H'(t) = -\hat B\, f(t)$ and ask how the
expectation value of some observable $\hat A$ changes. To first order in $f$,

$$
\delta \langle \hat A(t)\rangle
= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} dt'\; \chi_{AB}(t-t')\, f(t')
$$ {#eq-linear-response}

with the retarded response function

$$
\chi_{AB}(t-t') = -\frac{i}{\hbar}\,\theta(t-t')\,
\big\langle \big[\hat A_H(t), \hat B_H(t')\big] \big\rangle_0 .
$$ {#eq-kubo}

Three things are doing all the work in @eq-kubo. The **commutator** is what
survives at first order in perturbation theory. The **step function** enforces
causality: no response before the kick. The **average** is taken in the
*unperturbed* equilibrium state — the response is a property of the system
alone, not of the probe.

In frequency space $\chi_{AB}(\omega)$ has poles at the excitation energies of
the system. Measuring a spectrum is measuring where those poles sit and how
strongly each couples to the probe.

## Why it is set up this way

Linear response is not an approximation about the system — it is an
approximation about the *probe*. It says the perturbation is weak enough that
the system's own eigenstates still organise the answer. That is why a response
function is transferable between experiments: the same $\chi$ appears whatever
apparatus supplies $f(t)$, as long as it couples through $\hat B$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation: the Kubo formula

Work in the interaction picture with $\hat H = \hat H_0 + \hat H'(t)$ and
$\hat H'(t) = -\hat B f(t)$. The state evolves as
$\lvert\psi(t)\rangle = \hat U(t)\lvert\psi_0\rangle$ with

$$
\hat U(t) = \mathcal{T}\exp\left[
-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{t} dt'\, \hat H'_H(t')
\right]
\approx 1 + \frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{t} dt'\, \hat B_H(t') f(t') .
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\langle \hat A(t)\rangle
&= \langle \psi_0 \rvert \hat U^\dagger(t)\, \hat A_H(t)\, \hat U(t) \lvert \psi_0\rangle \\
&\approx \langle \hat A_H(t)\rangle_0
+ \frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{t} dt'\, f(t')
\big\langle \big[\hat B_H(t'), \hat A_H(t)\big] \big\rangle_0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the equilibrium value, swapping the commutator order to absorb the
sign, and extending the upper limit to $+\infty$ with a $\theta(t-t')$ gives
@eq-kubo. Time-translation invariance of $\hat H_0$ makes $\chi$ depend on
$t-t'$ only — which is exactly what fails out of equilibrium, and why
propagators there need
[two independent times](../why-two-times/index.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Aside: causality, analyticity, Kramers–Kronig

The $\theta(t-t')$ makes $\chi(\omega)$ analytic in the upper half plane.
Closing a contour there relates real and imaginary parts:

$$
\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathcal{P}\!\!
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} d\omega'\,
\frac{\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega} .
$$

This is why refraction and absorption are not independent measurements, and why
a measured absorption spectrum truncated at finite frequency yields a biased
refractive index. Causality alone forces it; no model is involved.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Aside: which $\hat A$ and $\hat B$ for optics

For light–matter coupling in the long-wavelength limit,
$\hat B = \hat{\mathbf P}$ (polarisation) and $f(t) = \mathbf E(t)$, so
$\chi$ is the electric susceptibility and
$\varepsilon(\omega) = 1 + \chi(\omega)$. Beyond dipole, or in the transverse
gauge, the natural pair is the current–current response, and translating
between the two conventions is a standard source of stray factors of $\omega$.
:::

## Common confusions

- **"The response function describes the experiment."** It describes the
  system. The experiment picks which $\hat A$, $\hat B$ and which $f(t)$.
- **"Poles of $\chi$ are single-particle energies."** They are energies of
  *neutral excitations* — differences between many-body states. That is why
  excitons appear in $\chi$ but not in a band structure.
- **"Linear response fails for strong fields, so it is a weak theory."** It
  fails for strong *probes*. It says nothing about how strongly the system's own
  constituents interact.
